questions.title: Anti-CCP antibody specificity
questions.question: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies are most frequently associated with:

explanations.A: Correct. Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibody is a specific serological marker for rheumatoid arthritis. Unlike rheumatoid factor, which is also seen in several unrelated diseases, anti-CCP's high specificity makes it valuable for confirming an RA diagnosis and for identifying RA early, before rheumatoid factor may have become positive. It is now a standard part of the rheumatoid arthritis diagnostic serology panel alongside rheumatoid factor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The seronegative spondyloarthritides (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthropathy) are defined by a NEGATIVE rheumatoid factor and are associated with HLA-B27, not with anti-CCP antibodies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Wegener's granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is associated with cytoplasmic ANCA (PR3-ANCA/cANCA), not anti-CCP antibodies.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progressive systemic sclerosis is associated with anti-centromere antibodies (limited form) or anti-Scl-70/topoisomerase I antibodies (diffuse form), not anti-CCP.

questions.learning_objective: Identify anti-CCP antibody as a specific serological marker for rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.title: RA typical feature
questions.question: The typical feature of rheumatoid arthritis is:

options.A: Always associated with a positive rheumatoid factor

explanations.A: Incorrect. Roughly 20-30% of RA patients are seronegative (rheumatoid-factor negative), particularly early in disease, so a positive RF is not universal and is not the defining clinical feature.
explanations.B: Correct. Prolonged morning stiffness — classically lasting at least one hour — is a hallmark clinical feature of rheumatoid arthritis, reflecting overnight accumulation of inflammatory synovial fluid and synovitis. It is one of the ACR 1987 classification criteria and is used clinically to distinguish inflammatory from mechanical joint pain, since mechanical/degenerative joint stiffness is typically brief.
explanations.C: Incorrect. RA characteristically involves the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints while sparing the distal interphalangeal joints; DIP involvement instead suggests osteoarthritis or psoriatic arthritis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. RA is a persistent, additive symmetrical polyarthritis, not a migratory one; migratory polyarthritis is more typical of rheumatic fever or gonococcal arthritis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise prolonged morning stiffness as a hallmark clinical feature of rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.title: Rheumatoid factor — true statements except
questions.question: All of the following are true about rheumatoid factor (RF) except:

options.A: It is present in most autoimmune diseases
options.B: It is present normally in the elderly and in pregnancy
options.C: Seronegative patients are excluded from having rheumatoid arthritis

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE, so not the answer). Rheumatoid factor is non-specific and is found in a range of autoimmune and chronic conditions besides RA, including SLE, Sjögren syndrome, scleroderma and chronic infections.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE, so not the answer). A low-titre positive rheumatoid factor can occur as a normal or incidental finding in elderly individuals and in pregnancy, without indicating rheumatoid arthritis.
explanations.C: Correct — this is the FALSE statement, and therefore the answer. Seronegative (RF-negative) patients are NOT excluded from a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. Roughly 20-30% of true RA patients are seronegative, especially early in the disease course, and the ACR criteria classify RA using a constellation of clinical and radiographic features, not rheumatoid factor alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since option C is a genuinely false statement, "none of the above" cannot be correct.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a seronegative rheumatoid-factor result does not exclude rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.title: Anaemia types in RA
questions.question: Which of the following types of anaemia could be caused by rheumatoid arthritis?

explanations.A: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own. Normocytic normochromic anaemia of chronic disease, from marrow suppression by ongoing inflammation, is the default RA-associated anaemia, but it is not the only mechanism RA produces — see option E.
explanations.B: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own. Microcytic hypochromic anaemia occurs in RA from chronic NSAID-induced gastrointestinal blood loss, but this is only one of several mechanisms — see option E.
explanations.C: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own. Megaloblastic anaemia occurs in RA from methotrexate-induced folate deficiency, but this is only one of several mechanisms — see option E.
explanations.D: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own. Marrow-suppressive drug toxicity (e.g. gold, methotrexate) or hypersplenism in Felty syndrome can produce more severe cytopenias including an aplastic picture, but this is only one of several mechanisms — see option E.
explanations.E: Correct. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause anaemia through multiple distinct mechanisms depending on the clinical context: normocytic normochromic anaemia of chronic disease from ongoing inflammation (the default pattern), microcytic hypochromic anaemia from NSAID-induced GI bleeding, megaloblastic anaemia from methotrexate-induced folate deficiency, and more severe marrow suppression (including an aplastic-range picture) from disease-modifying drug toxicity or hypersplenism in Felty syndrome. All of the listed types are recognised in RA, so "all of the above" is correct.

questions.learning_objective: Name the anaemia type behind a given RA clinical picture, distinguishing chronic-disease marrow suppression from the NSAID, methotrexate and Felty-syndrome mechanisms that also occur in RA.

questions.title: ACR 1987 RA criteria — exception
questions.question: All of the following are ARA (1987) criteria for the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a genuine criterion, so not the answer). Morning stiffness lasting more than one hour is one of the seven ACR 1987 criteria.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a genuine criterion, so not the answer). A positive rheumatoid factor is one of the seven ACR 1987 criteria.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a genuine criterion, so not the answer). Subcutaneous (rheumatoid) nodules are one of the seven ACR 1987 criteria.
explanations.D: Correct — this is the answer. The ACR 1987 criteria require SYMMETRICAL joint swelling, not asymmetrical arthritis; asymmetrical arthritis inverts the actual criterion rather than merely being absent from the list. This is the specific trap the question is built around, since it inverts the true criterion rather than merely omitting it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify which item in a list of proposed ACR-1987-criteria features is not genuine, recognising that the true criterion is symmetrical joint swelling.

questions.title: Acute gout — case diagnosis
questions.question: A 30-year-old overweight, hyperactive male, taking a thiazide diuretic and smoking, develops acute pain in his left foot around the big toe. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. DVT presents with unilateral calf/leg swelling, pain and warmth, not with acute pain localised specifically around the first metatarsophalangeal joint (the great toe).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tendonitis produces pain along a tendon on movement or palpation rather than acute joint-centred pain, and does not fit this constellation of gout risk factors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteoarthritis is a chronic, gradually progressive degenerative condition, not an acute presentation, and does not typically strike the great toe acutely in this way.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cellulitis is a skin/soft-tissue infection with diffuse erythema and systemic signs, not classically centred on a single joint with this specific risk-factor profile.
explanations.E: Correct. This vignette is the classic presentation of acute gouty arthritis: a man with the recognised risk factors — obesity, a thiazide diuretic (which reduces renal urate excretion), and smoking/lifestyle factors — presenting with sudden, acute pain around the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe (podagra). Thiazide diuretics are a well-known precipitant of hyperuricaemia and acute gout attacks.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise acute gout from a case combining male sex, a precipitating drug (thiazide diuretic) and an acutely inflamed first MTP joint.

questions.title: Gout — supportive investigation
questions.question: For the patient above with suspected acute gout, which is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. Serum uric acid is raised in most gout patients and is the standard supportive laboratory investigation used alongside the clinical picture to support a diagnosis of gout, even though joint aspiration with polarized-light microscopy remains the gold-standard confirmatory test. It is used alongside the clinical picture, even though joint aspiration with crystal microscopy remains the gold-standard confirmatory test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A complete blood count is nonspecific — it may show a mild leucocytosis in an acute attack but does not confirm gout.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ESR is a nonspecific marker of inflammation, raised in many conditions, and does not confirm gout specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Niacin (vitamin B3) is unrelated to gout diagnosis; in fact niacin therapy can itself raise uric acid levels, but it is not a diagnostic test.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Alpha-fetoprotein is a tumour marker (used in hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours) and has no role in gout diagnosis.

questions.learning_objective: Name serum uric acid as the standard supportive investigation for gout.

questions.title: Gout — best management advice
questions.question: What is the best advice for this patient (the thiazide-taking man with acute gout of the great toe)?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Weight reduction is a reasonable long-term lifestyle measure for gout risk, but it is not the immediate, specific action that addresses this patient's known precipitant.
explanations.B: Correct. This patient's gout attack has a clearly identifiable drug precipitant — the thiazide diuretic, which reduces renal excretion of uric acid and raises serum urate. Removing the precipitating drug is the specific, evidence-based management step in a patient whose gout is linked to a known trigger, alongside anti-inflammatory treatment of the acute attack.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Smoking cessation benefits general cardiovascular health but is not the specific intervention that addresses this patient's urate-raising drug.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer. Bed rest may provide symptomatic comfort during a severe attack but does not address the underlying precipitant and is not disease-modifying advice.

questions.learning_objective: Identify withdrawal of the precipitating drug (a thiazide diuretic) as the appropriate management step in a patient whose gout attack follows a known precipitant.

questions.title: Gout — gold-standard investigation
questions.question: The most diagnostic investigation of gout is:

options.A: Serum uric acid greater than 7 mg
options.B: Joint aspiration and polarized microscope analysis
options.C: X-ray of the first metatarsophalangeal joint

explanations.A: Incorrect. Serum uric acid is a supportive investigation, but it is neither diagnostic on its own (levels can be normal during an acute attack, or high in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia without gout) nor as specific as visualising the crystals directly.
explanations.B: Correct. Joint aspiration with polarized-light microscopy is the gold-standard investigation for gout, demonstrating needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals within the synovial fluid (often within neutrophils), which definitively confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes gout from pseudogout (rhomboid, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals). This directly visualises the crystals responsible for the disease, rather than relying on an indirect marker.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plain X-ray is often normal early in gout and, when abnormal (punched-out erosions), reflects chronic tophaceous disease rather than confirming an acute attack; it is not the gold-standard test.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since option B is a genuine, correct gold-standard investigation, "none of the above" cannot be correct.

questions.learning_objective: Choose joint aspiration and polarized-light microscopy as the gold-standard investigation confirming gout.

questions.title: Boutonniere deformity mechanism
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the buttonhole (boutonniere) deformity?

options.A: Flexion of both the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints
options.B: Flexion of the proximal and hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal joint
options.C: Hyperextension of the proximal and flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint
options.D: Hyperextension of both the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints

explanations.A: Incorrect. Flexion of both joints together is not the boutonniere pattern; the DIP joint is specifically hyperextended, not flexed.
explanations.B: Correct. The boutonniere (buttonhole) deformity is flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint with hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. It results from rupture of the extensor tendon's central slip over the PIP joint, which allows the lateral bands to slip volarward, so the joint head "buttonholes" through the extensor mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reversed pattern — PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion — describes swan-neck deformity, not boutonniere deformity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyperextension of both joints together is not the boutonniere pattern; the PIP joint is specifically flexed, not hyperextended.

questions.learning_objective: State the joint-level mechanism of the boutonniere deformity — PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension — and distinguish it from swan-neck deformity.

questions.title: Ankylosing spondylitis — young male case
questions.question: A young male teenager complains of lower back pain in the morning that relieves after one hour; his family history is positive. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. Ankylosing spondylitis classically presents in young men with insidious low back pain and morning stiffness that improves with activity/movement — here, relieved after about an hour — often with a positive family history, reflecting the strong HLA-B27 genetic association. The activity-related improvement in stiffness is the key discriminator from a mechanical back-pain cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute gout presents with sudden, severe monoarticular joint pain (classically the great toe), not chronic morning back stiffness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically affects small peripheral joints symmetrically, not primarily the axial skeleton/lower back in a young male.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Behçet disease presents with recurrent oral/genital ulcers, uveitis and variable systemic vasculitis, not primarily with inflammatory back pain.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lumbar spondylosis is a degenerative, mechanical condition typically of older patients, whose pain characteristically worsens rather than improves with activity — the opposite pattern to this case.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise ankylosing spondylitis from the combination of young age, male sex, activity-relieved back pain/morning stiffness, and a positive family history.

questions.title: Bouchard's nodes location
questions.question: Bouchard's nodes in osteoarthritis are seen in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The carpometacarpal (particularly the first, thumb-base) joint is a separate common site of osteoarthritis, but Bouchard's nodes are not located there.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Metacarpophalangeal joint involvement is more typical of rheumatoid arthritis than osteoarthritis, and is not the location of Bouchard's nodes.
explanations.C: Correct. Bouchard's nodes are bony nodes at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, seen in nodal osteoarthritis — the PIP-joint counterpart of Heberden's nodes at the DIP joint. This is the PIP-joint counterpart of Heberden's nodes, which instead sit at the DIP joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nodes at the distal interphalangeal joint are Heberden's nodes, not Bouchard's nodes — a commonly confused eponym pair.

questions.learning_objective: Localise Bouchard's nodes to the PIP joint and distinguish them from Heberden's nodes at the DIP joint.

questions.title: Heberden's nodules
questions.question: Heberden's nodules are seen in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Progressive systemic sclerosis presents with skin fibrosis, Raynaud's phenomenon and internal organ involvement, not Heberden's nodules.
explanations.B: Correct. Heberden's nodules are bony nodes at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, seen in nodal osteoarthritis, reflecting osteophyte formation at that joint. This is the DIP-joint counterpart of Bouchard's nodes, which instead sit at the PIP joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dermatomyositis presents with proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules), not Heberden's nodules.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium-vessel vasculitis with systemic and organ-specific manifestations, unrelated to Heberden's nodules.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Gout presents with acute crystal-induced joint inflammation and, in chronic disease, tophi, not Heberden's nodules, which are a degenerative osteoarthritis finding.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Heberden's nodules as a distal interphalangeal joint finding of osteoarthritis.

questions.title: Ankylosing spondylitis — back, hip and shoulder case
questions.question: A 20-year-old man began to note persistent lower back pain and stiffness that diminishes with activity. He also developed hip and shoulder arthritis and is bothered by decreased lumbar spine mobility. He has no other major medical problems. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. This is a classic ankylosing spondylitis presentation: a young man with persistent inflammatory back pain and stiffness that improves with activity, progressive involvement of the proximal (hip, shoulder) joints, and diminished lumbar spine mobility — all consistent with axial spondyloarthropathy. The proximal-joint (hip, shoulder) involvement alongside axial disease further supports this diagnosis over a purely peripheral arthritis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CPPD (pseudogout) typically presents as acute or chronic crystal arthritis of large peripheral joints (knee, wrist), not with this axial, activity-improved back pain pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lyme disease presents with erythema migrans, systemic symptoms, and later intermittent large-joint arthritis following a tick bite, not this chronic axial pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative condition of older patients, and its pain characteristically worsens rather than improves with activity — the opposite pattern to this case.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically causes symmetrical small peripheral joint disease, not primarily axial/back disease with activity-improved stiffness.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise ankylosing spondylitis from activity-improved axial pain plus hip/shoulder involvement in a young man.

questions.title: DIP joint classic involvement
questions.question: The terminal (distal) interphalangeal joint is classically involved in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically spares the distal interphalangeal joint, involving the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reactive arthritis typically causes an asymmetric large-joint oligoarthritis (knees, ankles) plus enthesitis, not classic DIP-predominant disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Felty syndrome is a variant of rheumatoid arthritis (splenomegaly, neutropenia) and follows RA's own joint pattern, not DIP-predominant disease.
explanations.D: Correct. Psoriatic arthritis has a distinct pattern that predominantly involves the distal interphalangeal joints, associated with psoriatic nail changes (pitting, ridging, hyperkeratosis) — a key feature distinguishing it from rheumatoid arthritis, which spares the DIP joint. This DIP-predominant pattern is one of several recognised psoriatic-arthritis patterns, alongside an asymmetrical oligoarticular form that is actually more common overall.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the distal interphalangeal joint as the classic site of a named psoriatic-arthritis pattern.

questions.title: DVT with recurrent abortion — antiphospholipid syndrome
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a deep vein thrombosis. Her previous history included investigation for repeated abortions. Investigations revealed: Hb 12.8, WBC normal, platelets low. Which of the following investigations is most likely to be abnormal?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperhomocysteinaemia is a recognised, but much less common, cause of thrombosis and recurrent miscarriage than antiphospholipid syndrome, and does not classically produce thrombocytopenia.
explanations.B: Correct. This vignette — recurrent thrombosis (DVT), a history of recurrent pregnancy loss, and thrombocytopenia — is the classic triad of antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune disease in which antibodies form against acidic (negatively charged) phospholipids, predisposing to both venous/arterial thrombosis and pregnancy complications. Antiphospholipid antibody testing (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I) would be the most likely abnormal, diagnostic investigation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An indium-labelled white cell scan is used to localise occult infection or inflammation, not to investigate thrombosis with recurrent miscarriage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A platelet function test assesses platelet activity/aggregation, not the underlying autoimmune cause of this patient's thrombosis and pregnancy loss.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Protein C deficiency is a recognised inherited thrombophilia, but it is a less likely explanation than antiphospholipid syndrome given this patient's combination of recurrent miscarriage AND low platelets, both classic antiphospholipid syndrome features.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise antiphospholipid syndrome from the combination of thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage and thrombocytopenia.

questions.title: HLA-B27 — not associated with
questions.question: HLA-B27 tissue typing is NOT associated with:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS associated, so not the answer). The axial form of psoriatic arthropathy carries an HLA-B27 association, as one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS associated, so not the answer). Ankylosing spondylitis has the strongest HLA-B27 association of this group, present in roughly 90-95% of patients.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS associated, so not the answer). Reiter's syndrome/reactive arthritis is HLA-B27 associated in the majority of cases (around 80%).
explanations.D: Correct. Behçet syndrome is a distinct vasculitis (recurrent oral/genital ulcers, uveitis) that is not part of the seronegative spondyloarthropathy family and is instead associated with HLA-B51, not HLA-B27. It is genetically distinct from the seronegative spondyloarthropathy family that HLA-B27 marks.

questions.learning_objective: Name which condition among a list of seronegative-arthritis-family diseases is NOT HLA-B27 associated.

questions.title: Nodal osteoarthritis epidemiology
questions.question: Nodal osteoarthritis is common in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hypertension is not the epidemiological association classically taught for nodal generalised osteoarthritis.
explanations.B: Correct. Nodal generalised osteoarthritis (with Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes) is markedly more common in postmenopausal women, reflecting a hormonal and genetic predisposition in this group. This reflects a hormonal and genetic predisposition distinct from osteoarthritis's other, non-nodal forms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diabetes mellitus is a secondary-osteoarthritis risk factor in some classifications, but is not the classic epidemiological association for the nodal generalised pattern specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gout is itself a separate cause of secondary osteoarthritis in some schemes, but is not the epidemiological group classically linked to nodal osteoarthritis.

questions.learning_objective: State that nodal generalised osteoarthritis is characteristically more common in postmenopausal women.

questions.title: Acute monoarthritis workup
questions.question: A 62-year-old hypertensive man presents with pain, redness and swelling in the right knee, which started 12 hours ago. There is a family history of hypertension and joint problems. What investigation is most important in identifying the cause of this patient's knee symptoms?

explanations.A: Incorrect. ESR is a nonspecific inflammatory marker that does not identify the specific cause of an acute monoarthritis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. HLA status is relevant to the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, not to the urgent workup of a new acute monoarthritis, where excluding infection takes priority.
explanations.C: Correct. In any new acute monoarthritis, joint aspiration is the key next investigation — examining the fluid's appearance, cell count, Gram stain/culture, and crystal microscopy — primarily to exclude septic arthritis (the differential that cannot wait) before a crystal or degenerative cause is assumed. Excluding infection is the priority because delayed treatment of septic arthritis can rapidly destroy the joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plain radiology is often normal in an acute presentation and does not identify an infective or crystal cause as directly as joint fluid analysis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Serology is more relevant to a chronic inflammatory arthritis workup than to the urgent evaluation of a new, acute, single hot joint.

questions.learning_objective: Choose joint aspiration as the appropriate next step in a new acute monoarthritis, recognising that excluding septic arthritis takes priority.

questions.title: Limited scleroderma survival
questions.question: The survival rate of limited scleroderma is approximately:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This underestimates the survival of limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome).
explanations.B: Incorrect. This underestimates the survival of limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome).
explanations.C: Correct. Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome — calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) carries a substantially better prognosis than diffuse systemic sclerosis, with roughly 70% ten-year survival, because its skin-and-peripheral-vessel-predominant disease specifically spares the severe early internal-organ involvement seen in diffuse disease. This is notably better than the outlook for diffuse systemic sclerosis, which involves earlier, more severe internal-organ disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This overestimates the survival figure taught for limited scleroderma.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This overestimates the survival figure taught for limited scleroderma.

questions.learning_objective: State that limited scleroderma/CREST carries roughly 70% ten-year survival, better than diffuse systemic sclerosis.

questions.title: RA — bad prognostic factors
questions.question: Which of the following is considered a bad prognosis in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.C: Positive rheumatoid factor and HLA-DR4 association

explanations.A: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own. Female sex is one recognised poor-prognosis marker in RA, but not the only one — see option E.
explanations.B: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own — note the wording: a RAPIDLY (not slowly) progressive course is the poor-prognosis pattern, and this option is still bundled correctly under "all of the above" as one of the factors this bank's own answer groups together; see option E for the complete answer.
explanations.C: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own. A strongly positive rheumatoid factor and HLA-DR4 carriage are each independently recognised poor-prognosis markers in RA, but neither is the only one — see option E.
explanations.D: Partially correct, but incomplete on its own. Anaemia within the first three months of disease onset is one recognised poor-prognosis marker in RA, but not the only one — see option E.
explanations.E: Correct. Poor prognostic factors in rheumatoid arthritis include female sex, an aggressive disease course, a strongly positive rheumatoid factor, anaemia within the first 3 months of disease, and HLA-DR4 carriage — the bank's own printed answer groups these together as a recognised cluster of adverse markers. The bank's own printed answer groups these together as a recognised cluster of adverse markers rather than treating any single one as sufficient alone.

questions.learning_objective: List the recognised poor-prognosis markers in RA and recognise a vignette naming several of them together.

Option B is printed as "Slowly progressive course" in the source; standard teaching names a RAPID course as poor-prognosis. questions.title: Pseudogout crystal
questions.question: Pseudogout (chondrocalcinosis) is associated with deposition of crystals of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Calcium oxalate crystal deposition is associated with conditions such as ethylene glycol poisoning and some renal stones, not pseudogout.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Monosodium urate is the crystal deposited in gout, not pseudogout — a commonly confused pair the question is testing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Calcium phosphate is not the classically taught crystal of pseudogout; calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate is.
explanations.D: Correct. Pseudogout (chondrocalcinosis) is caused by deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in joints, seen as rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals on polarized-light microscopy — distinct from gout's needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals. These crystals are rhomboid-shaped and weakly positively birefringent on polarized-light microscopy, distinguishing pseudogout from gout's needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals.

questions.learning_objective: Name calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate as the crystal deposited in pseudogout.

questions.title: Not used for acute gouty arthritis
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT used to treat acute gouty arthritis?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS used for the acute attack, so not the answer). Corticosteroids such as prednisolone are used to treat an acute gout flare when NSAIDs are contraindicated or ineffective.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS used for the acute attack, so not the answer). Colchicine is a first-line agent for acute gouty arthritis, reducing leucocyte migration and inflammatory mediator release.
explanations.C: Correct. Allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is chronic/maintenance urate-lowering therapy, not acute-attack treatment. Starting it during an acute flare can precipitate or worsen the attack by mobilising urate, so it is begun only about four weeks after the last attack has settled, with colchicine cover.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS used for the acute attack, so not the answer). NSAIDs such as indomethacin are standard first-line anti-inflammatory treatment for an acute gout attack.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise allopurinol as excluded from acute-gout treatment, understanding the risk of precipitating/worsening the attack.
questions.author_notes: Source prints only 3 options (Prednisolone, Colchicine, Allopurinol) with no lettering; the seed/emit-mcq contract requires 4-5 options, so a 4th distractor (Indomethacin, an NSAID also used for acute gout per src_a51388c9442af6f01df5 p.34) was added from the module's own governed lecture, not invented from outside knowledge. This does not change the printed key (Allopurinol/C remains the sole answer); flagged transparently rather than silently padded.

questions.title: Infliximab target
questions.question: Infliximab is directed against:

explanations.A: Incorrect. ICAM-1 is not infliximab's target; it is a cell-adhesion molecule targeted by different agents (e.g. some monoclonal antibodies used in other inflammatory conditions).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interleukin-2 is targeted by agents such as basiliximab (used in transplant immunosuppression), not infliximab.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interleukin-6 is targeted by agents such as tocilizumab, not infliximab.
explanations.D: Correct. Infliximab is a biological response modifier that acts as a TNF-alpha inhibitor, blocking one of the key inflammatory cytokines driving rheumatoid arthritis. Biologics such as infliximab act faster than conventional disease-modifying drugs and are given by infusion, repeated at increasing intervals.

questions.learning_objective: Name TNF-alpha as the target of infliximab.

questions.title: Which drug is not a DMARD
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD)?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a DMARD, so not the answer). Hydroxychloroquine is a conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug, often used in mild RA.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a DMARD, so not the answer). Leflunomide is a conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug used when methotrexate is not tolerated.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a DMARD, so not the answer). Sulfasalazine is a conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug.
explanations.D: Correct. Naproxen is an NSAID — an anti-inflammatory drug that controls symptoms by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis but does not modify the underlying disease course, so it is not classified as a DMARD even though it is used to treat RA symptoms. NSAIDs and DMARDs are defined by mechanism, not by which disease they treat, which is exactly the distinction this question tests.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the DMARD drug class from NSAIDs, recognising that a symptom-control anti-inflammatory drug is not automatically disease-modifying.
